extracted.intended_audience: readers and writers interested in literary humour, satire, and performance (general literary audience; students of humour)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting principles and evaluative statements about humour as expressed in a literary/fictional passage (Chesterton). Focuses on what counts as humour, how it should be received, and techniques for producing it in public and anecdotal forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test of humour (anecdote reception)
rubrics_metrics.description: "That story," he said reverently, "is the test of humour."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chesterton (via Quin) asserts that the 'great anecdote' is received in silence, 'like a benediction.' By contrast, 'Only coarse humour is received with pot-house applause.' Example anecdote given (body wearing patent-leather boots; return ticket to Maidstone) is presented as a specimen of the high anecdote whose proper reception is quiet, not noisy approval. Implication for evaluation/production: the best jokes may elicit thoughtful, silent appreciation rather than raucous laughter; applause can indicate a lower, coarser form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subtlety / mysterious humour (invisibility as virtue)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Hitherto it was the ruin of a joke that people did not see it. Now it is the sublime victory of a joke that people do not see it."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quin claims modern humour can succeed precisely by being so delicate that people 'do not see it' — the joke's victory is its imperceptibility. This valorises subtle, elusive humour that operates beneath obvious perception. For creators: aim for layers or sly inversions that may escape instant recognition; for evaluators: value humour that registers as a 'sublime victory' even if it does not produce immediate, audible response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sense of humour = capacity to see humour in ordinary things
rubrics_metrics.description: "If I say that you cannot see the humour of that tree... if I say that you were guilty of the supreme blasphemy of looking at that tree and not seeing in it a new religion... But if I say that you cannot see the humour of that tree, and that I see the humour of it--my God! you will roll about at my feet."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Humour is presented as a 'weird and delicate sense' that perceives the comic in everyday objects (trees, iron railings, fields of corn, sunsets). Instructional: cultivate a perceptive eye that reframes commonplace sights as comic revelations. Evaluation: judge humour partly on the creator's ability to reveal an incongruous or comic aspect in the mundane.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reversal of the obvious / inversion as core mechanism
rubrics_metrics.description: "All ceremony consists in the reversal of the obvious... The reversal of the obvious is as near as we can come to ritual with our imperfect apparatus."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chesterton links ceremony and humour: both rely on inverting expectations (e.g., dressing tails in front). The comic effect often arises from deliberately reversing normal roles, behaviours, or presentations. Guidance for practice: use inversion/subversion (role reversals, opposite behaviours) as a reliable engine of humour; for critique: identify whether inversion reveals insight or merely absurdity without meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public/private inversion as a policy of humour
rubrics_metrics.description: "My sense of humour suggests the reversal of the obvious; it suggests that one should be funny in public, and solemn in private."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A deliberate rule for performance: invert the usual privacy of humour by staging antics publicly and reserving seriousness for private spaces. This produces societal surprise and maximises comedic effect in public life. Evaluation note: effectiveness depends on contrast and the social stakes of public solemnity being breached.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physicality and visual absurdity (pantomime/slapstick)
rubrics_metrics.description: (Examples) Quin stands on his head, waves patent-leather boots in the air, hops on one leg, sits on another man's hat; "the man who sits on his hat in a pantomime is a long sight funnier than you are."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chesterton emphasizes bodily comedy and visible absurdity as powerful comedic techniques. Guidance: physical gestures, posture, pantomime and visible inversion can outstrip verbal wit in eliciting laughter. Anti-pattern: relying solely on talky or abstract points when physical action would land the humour more strongly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivation of humour as a devotion/discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: "Humour, my friends, is the one sanctity remaining to mankind... Exercises, spiritual exercises, will be set in it."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quin treats humour as a quasi-religious practice that can be trained and disciplined. Instruction: cultivate a habitual, ascetic attention to finding and refining comic perception (exercises to 'see' humour). Evaluation: value sustained practice and deliberate cultivation as indicators of serious comic art rather than mere caprice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paradox and aphoristic contradiction as comic device
rubrics_metrics.description: (Examples scattered) "The superstition of democracy is the worst of all." "We have become a despotism... the sane and enduring democracy is founded on the fact that all men are equally idiotic."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chesterton uses paradoxical, aphoristic statements — sharp contradictions that invert common moral or political assumptions — to produce comic and satirical effect. Guidance: craft pithy paradoxes that challenge accepted platitudes; evaluation: judge whether the paradox reveals insight or is merely provocative without substance.
